items.question: Why do you prioritize general intelligence in OpenAI’s pursuit of an automated researcher?
items.object: Generality in OpenAI’s pursuit of an automated researcher
items.answer: When we think about how we shape our research program at OpenAI, we seek to create intelligence that is very general. We drive towards this automated researcher as a priority, but we don't really think of it as, “Let's take these specific domains and deploy this technology there.” I think that is a way to make faster pointwise progress. But I think the potential for the really big discoveries and the most meaningful technology advancement comes from this generality.
quotes: When we think about how we shape our research program at OpenAI, we seek to create intelligence that is very general. We drive towards this automated researcher as a priority, but we don't really think of it as, “Let's take these specific domains and deploy this technology there.” I think that is a way to make faster pointwise progress. But I think the potential for the really big discoveries and the most meaningful technology advancement comes from this generality.

rubrics.text: The response states that targeting specific domains can produce faster progress within those domains.
The response identifies generality of intelligence as a source of potential for the biggest discoveries.

items.question: Where do you see especially promising opportunities to apply AI?
items.object: AI applications in medicine and research
items.answer: I think we see the technology is easier to apply in some domains than others. I think especially in places that combine a large amount of reasoning with a lot of domain knowledge and intuition seem very amenable to these systems. In particular, we see pretty incredible results on medicine, which is very encouraging. I have high hopes about that. Naturally, being a company of AI researchers, we think a lot about automating our own work. I don't think it's a given, but if AI can indeed reach a point where you can automate AI research, that is probably a very important thing to automate. And similarly, thinking about how it can help with automating research on AI alignment and safety.

items.question: Why do you regard solving all the problems on the International Mathematical Olympiad as a meaningful milestone for AI?
items.object: International Mathematical Olympiad results as a measure of AI capability
items.answer: I'm obviously impressed by the IMO results. In the past, when we were talking about the IMO, that was a few years ago, and we were still trying to figure out what our definition of AGI might be. One concept we were considering is solving all the problems on the math Olympiad. Why did that feel appropriate? If you have a model with such superior mathematical reasoning, then it should be able to disrupt a bunch of different domains that can be mathematically modeled.

items.question: How do you react to headlines interpreting AI's economic impact of 3% or 5% as evidence that progress is slowing?
items.object: Claims that AI progress is slowing based on its measured economic impact
items.answer: I was astounded by the progress. Sometimes I see those headlines where people say that the economic impact of AI is only 3% or 5%, and those headlines are often accompanied by comments like, “AI is slowing down,” or “People are overhyping AI so much and it's only like 3%, so what's up with that?” When I see headlines like this, I remember maybe 10 years ago I was working on natural language processing with deep learning, and back then it just didn't really work. I remember Jakob once came to test one of the technologies we were working on, trying to detect sentiment of sentences. He was trying, “This movie is bad,” correctly classified as negative; “This movie is good,” correctly classified as positive. Then he would say, “This movie is not bad,” and the model is like, “Oh, negative.”

items.question: How do you see the importance of scaling pre-training as reasoning models advance?
items.answer: I think one thing we always try to not underestimate is the importance of scaling. Even as we look at these reasoning models, it's not like the previous scaling paradigm of pre-training has vanished. I think we will see these things compound.
quotes: I think one thing we always try to not underestimate is the importance of scaling. Even as we look at these reasoning models, it's not like the previous scaling paradigm of pre-training has vanished. I think we will see these things compound.

rubrics.text: The response expresses the expectation that scaling pre-training and advances in reasoning models will have compounding benefits.

items.question: Why do you see models’ ability to work for a long time on a focused problem as a promising direction for AI progress?
items.object: Model persistence and longer reasoning horizons
items.answer: I think there's also new directions that we can move in. In particular, we were talking about extending the horizon that these models can plan for and reason over. If you look at it from the perspective of just compute spend, GPT-4 was doing some compute for every answer, to GPT-5 Pro, which maybe uses 10x, 20x, I don't know, some non-trivial but in some ways not that impressive amount of compute more, and can produce much better answers. On the scale of what amount of compute would you be willing to spend on a problem that actually matters to a lot of people, on progress on a medical research question, progress on developing the next generation of models, these are incomparably larger amounts. So I think that question of model persistence and ability to work for a very long time on a focused problem is a pretty clear next direction.

items.question: How do you envision automated research changing the pace of technical progress?
items.object: Automated research and its implications for technical progress
items.answer: My picture of how that would actually look like is, imagine a company of very capable researchers and engineers that is largely automated. Again, that is something that will interface with the world in all sorts of ways. It won't be just a black box; it will talk to people, it will take in inputs, it will run experiments. But having this potential for developing new technology and other artifacts—codebases, designs—I think can radically accelerate the pace of technical progress. I think that is something that we will feel, and we need to do a lot of work to get it right from a technical and societal perspective. But I think that is where I turn to. I think we should also expect a lot of progress on the actual interfaces that we interact with.

items.question: How do you expect people's emotional attachments to ChatGPT to develop as it becomes more capable?
items.answer: You know, we see ChatGPT can feel quite humanlike. We can form attachments with it. As it becomes more persistent, as it becomes capable of expressing itself in different forms and texts, I think those effects will become stronger, and again, that will be a very big and important conversation.

rubrics.text: The response predicts that greater persistence in ChatGPT will strengthen users’ emotional attachments to it.
The response predicts that ChatGPT’s ability to express itself in more varied forms will strengthen users’ emotional attachments to it.
